title: Nitrogen Everywhere, and Not a Bit to Use

scenes.visual: Title card 'Nitrogen Everywhere, and Not a Bit to Use' over the farm cutaway at dawn, grey paired dots drifting slowly in the sky. COLOUR MAP (both films): nitrogen gas = GREY PAIRED DOTS (two dots joined by a short bar) filling a big pale-grey sky 'tank'; usable nitrogen = small GREEN DOTS in light-blue soil water; sugar = an ORANGE arrow; the 'gate' = a small glowing GOLD clasp on the bar of every grey pair, holding its two dots together; only changers can snap a clasp open, and then the pair becomes green dots. Grey pairs drift freely everywhere, into soil, around roots and into nodules, still clasped; the gate is the clasp, not a place. Never draw a gate line at the soil surface. Setting: the same Virginia farm cutaway in every scene: soybeans on the left, corn on the right, woods with a white-tailed deer behind, a stream running off to the Chesapeake Bay. Plants, animals and microbes are cartoons; every cutaway is labelled 'schematic'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: The air around you is mostly nitrogen. So why does this cornfield need nitrogen added, while the soybeans next door often do not?
scenes.visual: Camera glides over the cornfield on the right; a farmer spreads fertilizer from a bag labelled 'nitrogen'. Pan left to the soybeans, no bag. On-screen: 'air: about 78% nitrogen'. Question card: 'Why does corn need nitrogen added, and soybeans often not?'
scenes.narration: The air around you is mostly nitrogen. So why does this cornfield need nitrogen added, while the soybeans next door often do not?

scenes.tts: First, why does a plant need nitrogen at all? A protein is a large molecule that builds cells and does much of its work. Proteins contain nitrogen. D N A, which carries the plant's instructions, contains nitrogen too.
scenes.caption: First, why does a plant need nitrogen at all? A protein is a large molecule that builds cells and does much of its work. Proteins contain nitrogen. DNA, which carries the plant's instructions, contains nitrogen too.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a corn leaf, then into one cartoon cell. Two labelled blocks float inside: 'protein' and 'DNA', each studded with small green tags labelled 'nitrogen'. New leaf buds sprout as tags arrive.
scenes.narration: First, why does a plant need nitrogen at all? A protein is a large molecule that builds cells and does much of its work. Proteins contain nitrogen. DNA, which carries the plant's instructions, contains nitrogen too.

scenes.tts: So without nitrogen, a plant cannot build new proteins or grow new leaves.
scenes.visual: The tags stop arriving; the bud stalls and the leaf yellows slightly. Caption: 'no nitrogen, no new leaves'.
scenes.narration: So without nitrogen, a plant cannot build new proteins or grow new leaves.

scenes.tts: Now pull back to the sky above one field. It holds a huge amount of nitrogen gas. The soybeans growing there hold only a tiny bit.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls up above one square of field labelled '1 hectare'. A tall grey column of air rises over it and a counter fills: 'about 78,000 tonnes of nitrogen'. Beside it a tiny green stack: 'soybeans above the ground, one Michigan study: about 0.19 tonnes'. The stack is barely visible next to the column.
scenes.narration: Now pull back to the sky above one field. It holds a huge amount of nitrogen gas. The soybeans growing there hold only a tiny bit.

scenes.tts: But corn cannot use nitrogen gas. Neither can a deer, or you. Grey pairs drift down into the soil, right past the corn's roots. Each pair stays clasped shut. The gate is locked.
scenes.visual: Grey paired dots drift past the corn's leaves and down into the soil around its roots; each pair's GOLD clasp stays shut and a tiny padlock icon flickers on one clasp. The roots take none of them. Caption: 'nitrogen gas: locked shut'.
scenes.narration: But corn cannot use nitrogen gas. Neither can a deer, or you. Grey pairs drift down into the soil, right past the corn's roots. Each pair stays clasped shut. The gate is locked.

scenes.tts: Plants can use only usable nitrogen. That is nitrogen changed out of the gas into small particles that plants can take in. Roots take most from soil water. Next to the sky, this green pool is small.
scenes.visual: In the soil, a shallow light-blue pool of soil water with scattered GREEN dots, labelled 'usable nitrogen'. Clasped grey pairs float through the soil too, unused. Corn roots draw a few green dots up. The camera compares: huge grey sky tank above, small green pool below.
scenes.narration: Plants can use only usable nitrogen. That is nitrogen changed out of the gas into small particles that plants can take in. Roots take most from soil water. Next to the sky, this green pool is small.

scenes.tts: So who opens the gate? Lightning opens it a little, in a flash. Factories that make fertilizer open it wide. Fertilizer is material farmers add to soil to supply nutrients.
scenes.visual: A lightning bolt strikes; the GOLD clasps on a few grey pairs near the flash snap open and those pairs fall into the soil as green dots. Then a cartoon factory takes in a stream of grey pairs, snaps their clasps and fills a fertilizer bag; the bag pours many green dots onto the cornfield. Labels: 'lightning: a little', 'fertilizer factory: a lot'.
scenes.narration: So who opens the gate? Lightning opens it a little, in a flash. Factories that make fertilizer open it wide. Fertilizer is material farmers add to soil to supply nutrients.

scenes.tts: Some bacteria open the gate too. Bacteria are tiny living things, each made of one cell. Some kinds live free in the soil. Each changer turns grey pairs into green dots.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the soil: tiny rod-shaped cartoon bacteria labelled 'bacteria (one cell each), schematic'. A clasped grey pair enters one, the clasp snaps open and green dots come out. Summary row of three icons, lightning, factory, bacterium, each with 'grey pair → green dots'.
scenes.narration: Some bacteria open the gate too. Bacteria are tiny living things, each made of one cell. Some kinds live free in the soil. Each changer turns grey pairs into green dots.

scenes.tts: Now picture soil with almost no usable nitrogen. Corn and soybeans stand in the same air. Which one could still grow well? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: The green pool drains to a few dots. Corn on the right, soybean on the left, same grey sky above. Pause card: 'Almost no usable nitrogen in the soil. Which could still grow well?' with buttons 'corn' and 'soybean'. Ring timer.
scenes.narration: Now picture soil with almost no usable nitrogen. Corn and soybeans stand in the same air. Which one could still grow well? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Pause card holds; ring timer runs down.

scenes.tts: The soybean. Dig it up and shake off the soil. See the small round bumps on its roots? Each one is a root nodule, and it is packed with bacteria.
scenes.visual: A cartoon hand lifts the soybean; soil falls away to show small round bumps on the roots, labelled 'root nodule'. Zoom into one nodule, labelled 'schematic': packed with rod-shaped bacteria.
scenes.narration: The soybean. Dig it up and shake off the soil. See the small round bumps on its roots? Each one is a root nodule, and it is packed with bacteria.

scenes.tts: Inside the nodule, the bacteria take in nitrogen gas and pass usable nitrogen to the plant. The soybean carries its own gate opener, right on its roots.
scenes.visual: Clasped grey pairs seep into the nodule from the soil; inside, their GOLD clasps snap open and green dots flow out along a green arrow up the root into the stem. Caption: 'a private gate opener'.
scenes.narration: Inside the nodule, the bacteria take in nitrogen gas and pass usable nitrogen to the plant. The soybean carries its own gate opener, right on its roots.

scenes.tts: The plant sends sugar from its leaves down to the nodules. Root cells there change the sugar into food the bacteria can use.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE arrow labelled 'sugar' runs from the leaves down the stem into the nodule; at the nodule it turns into small orange crumbs labelled 'food for bacteria'. The GREEN arrow keeps flowing up. Two arrows, opposite directions, labelled 'partners'.
scenes.narration: The plant sends sugar from its leaves down to the nodules. Root cells there change the sugar into food the bacteria can use.

scenes.tts: Corn has no root nodules. It can draw only on the green dots already in the soil. That is why corn farmers usually add nitrogen to their fields.
scenes.visual: Pan to the corn: its roots, dug up, are smooth with no bumps. Its roots pull the last few green dots out of the pool. The farmer's fertilizer bag returns and refills the pool with green dots.
scenes.narration: Corn has no root nodules. It can draw only on the green dots already in the soil. That is why corn farmers usually add nitrogen to their fields.

scenes.tts: So the air's nitrogen is not the problem. The gate is. Plants need usable nitrogen, not the nitrogen gas in the air. Where nitrogen runs short, usable nitrogen sets how much a field can grow.
scenes.visual: Wide shot: huge grey sky tank of clasped pairs, small green pool in the soil. The pool level rises and the plants grow taller with it; the grey tank stays the same. Caption: 'where nitrogen runs short'.
scenes.narration: So the air's nitrogen is not the problem. The gate is. Plants need usable nitrogen, not the nitrogen gas in the air. Where nitrogen runs short, usable nitrogen sets how much a field can grow.

scenes.tts: But do the bumps really add nitrogen to a soybean crop? The lesson tests that with real field data.
scenes.visual: A soybean root with nodules beside one without, both with a large question mark. Caption: 'Do the bumps really add nitrogen?'. No data shown.
scenes.narration: But do the bumps really add nitrogen to a soybean crop? The lesson tests that with real field data.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line: 'Plants need usable nitrogen, not the nitrogen gas in air.'
